college.stem: In tests of memory for lists of items such as letters, what is found about lists whose items sound alike?
options: They were recalled worse than lists of different-sounding items, which points to a speech-based memory code.
They were recalled worse than lists of different-looking items, which points to a purely visual memory code.
They were recalled better than lists of different-sounding items, because shared sounds act as helpful cues.
They were recalled just as well as lists of different-sounding items, so sound plays no role in memory.
college.why: Sound-alike lists are recalled worse, the phonological similarity effect, so people recode into a speech form. The visual-code, benefit, and no-difference options contradict that result.

simple.stem: What is found about recall of lists with similar-sounding items?
options: Similar-sounding lists were recalled worse than lists of different-sounding items.
Similar-sounding lists were recalled better than lists of different-sounding items.
Similar-looking lists were recalled worse than lists of different-looking items.
Similar-sounding lists were recalled no differently than lists of different-sounding items.
simple.why: Similar-sounding items carry a recall cost. Better recall, a look-alike cost, or no difference are not what is found.

college.stem: Participants in an experiment repeated an irrelevant sound over and over while studying a list. Why was this condition included?
options: It kept the speech-recoding process occupied, so researchers could see whether the sound-similarity cost depended on recoding.
It increased the amount of rehearsal, so researchers could measure the largest possible memory span.
It made items look more alike, so researchers could measure visual confusion errors.
It reduced attention to the list, so researchers could measure raw sensory memory.
college.why: Repeating a sound keeps the articulatory control process busy, so visual input cannot be turned into a speech code. This tests whether the similarity effect relies on that recoding. The condition blocks rehearsal rather than increasing it, and it is not aimed at visual similarity or sensory memory.

simple.stem: What was the purpose of the articulatory suppression condition in this kind of experiment?
options: To stop people from converting what they see into a speech code.
To help people rehearse the list more times before recall.
To make the items on the list look more similar to each other.
To measure how long a sensory trace lasts after the list ends.
simple.why: Suppression keeps the articulatory control process busy so recoding cannot occur. It does not boost rehearsal, change appearance, or measure sensory trace length.

college.stem: Someone silently looks at the letters C, T, P, B, G, D and then tries to recall them. Which errors fit the phonological similarity effect?
options: Confusions between letters that sound alike, because the letters were recoded into a speech form.
Confusions between letters that look alike, because the letters were kept in a purely visual form.
Errors on the first letters only, because early items are always forgotten first.
No errors at all, because silent viewing keeps letters out of a speech code.
college.why: Sound-alike letters get mixed up because silent input is recoded into speech. A visual code would produce look-alike confusions, and nothing in the effect predicts only early-item errors or perfect recall.

simple.stem: Why do people mix up the letters B and T more than the letters B and O when recalling a silently viewed list?
options: Because B and T sound alike, and people recode what they see into a speech form.
Because B and T look alike, and people keep letters in a purely visual form.
Because B and T are the same size on screen, and same-size items blur together.
Because B and T are harder to say aloud, and hard-to-say letters decay faster.
simple.why: People recode visual input into a speech code, so sound-alike items collide. B and T sound alike, while B and O do not. Visual form, size and ease of speech are not the explanation.

college.stem: In a short-term memory task, Roodenrys et al. (2002) varied how many similar words a word has. What was their result?
options: Words with many close neighbors were recalled better than words with few close neighbors.
Words with few close neighbors were recalled better than words with many close neighbors.
Words with many and few close neighbors were recalled equally well.
Words with many close neighbors were recalled better only after a long delay.
college.why: Roodenrys et al. (2002) found a large-neighborhood advantage, which shows that stored knowledge about words helps short-term recall. The reverse pattern and the null pattern are not what they found, and a long delay was not the key factor.

simple.stem: What did Roodenrys et al. (2002) find about words from large neighborhoods?
options: They were recalled better than words from small neighborhoods.
They were recalled worse than words from small neighborhoods.
They were recalled the same as words from small neighborhoods.
They were recalled well only when heard rather than seen.
simple.why: Large-neighborhood words were recalled better. Worse recall, equal recall, or a hearing-only benefit are not the reported finding.

college.stem: Which example shows two words that are neighbors in an orthographic neighborhood?
options: The words cat and bat, which differ by a single letter.
The words cat and kitten, which share a similar meaning.
The words cat and dog, which are both common pets.
The words cat and catalog, which differ by several letters.
college.why: Orthographic neighbors differ by one letter, as cat and bat do. Shared meaning, category membership, or large spelling differences do not make words neighbors.

simple.stem: What is a word's neighborhood?
options: The set of words that differ from it by one letter or one sound.
The set of words that appeared just before it in a list.
The set of words that mean the same thing as it does.
The set of words that are spelled with the same first letter.
simple.why: Neighborhood means words differing by one letter or sound. The other options describe list order, meaning, or first letters, which are different properties.

college.stem: Two groups are tested on word lists. One list uses words with many neighbors and the other uses words with few neighbors, and the groups differ in span. What should a researcher conclude about using span as a capacity measure?
options: The score reflects long-term memory influences as well as capacity, so it is not a pure measure.
The score reflects only capacity, because word type cannot influence short-term memory.
The score reflects only attention, because neighborhood alters how closely people listen.
The score reflects only rehearsal speed, because large neighborhoods are said faster.
college.why: Neighborhood is a long-term memory property, so a span that changes with it is not a pure capacity measure. Capacity-only, attention-only, and rehearsal-speed-only explanations ignore the long-term memory contribution.

simple.stem: What does the neighborhood size effect imply about memory span?
options: Memory span is not a pure measure of short-term capacity.
Memory span is a pure measure of short-term capacity.
Memory span measures only the speed of speech.
Memory span measures only sensory memory.
simple.why: Long-term memory factors affect span, so it is not pure capacity. The other options claim purity or reduce span to a single unrelated process.

college.stem: In the Brown-Peterson task, counting backwards is very different from remembering letters. Which account of the forgetting did the researchers set aside?
options: Forgetting is caused by interference from other material, not by simple fading.
Forgetting is caused by simple fading, not by interference from other material.
Forgetting is caused by poor attention at encoding, not by either fading or interference.
Forgetting is caused by damage to the sensory store, not by interference.
college.why: Interference seemed an unlikely cause because the counting differs so much from the letters. Attention-at-encoding and sensory-store explanations were not the alternative being weighed.

simple.stem: In the Brown-Peterson task, which explanation of the forgetting did the researchers judge unlikely?
options: Interference from other material.
Decay over time.
Poor attention at encoding.
Weak sensory input.
simple.why: Counting backwards is so unlike remembering letters that interference seemed unlikely. The other options are not what they set aside.

college.stem: A researcher wants to see whether short-term memory fades with time alone. Why would the researcher fill the delay with counting rather than with more letters to learn?
options: Counting prevents rehearsal while, the researchers reasoned, adding little interference, since it is very different from the to-be-remembered letters.
Counting allows extra rehearsal, since numbers are easy to say while holding the letters.
Counting adds similar material, which gives a stronger test of interference.
Counting increases attention to the letters, which makes forgetting less likely.
college.why: A dissimilar distractor blocks rehearsal without adding much interference, so forgetting points to decay. More letters would introduce interference, and counting does not enable rehearsal.

simple.stem: Why was counting used as the distraction in the Brown-Peterson task?
options: It stops rehearsal and was judged unlikely to cause interference.
It helps people rehearse the letters.
It makes the letters easier to see.
It adds more letters to confuse memory.
simple.why: Counting blocks rehearsal and is too unlike the letters to interfere. It does not help rehearsal, vision, or add letters.

college.stem: A participant sees three consonants, counts for a long time, and then cannot recall them. Which statement best fits the conclusion Peterson and Peterson (1959) drew from the Brown-Peterson task?
options: The letters faded from short-term memory because rehearsal was blocked for too long.
The letters were held safely because counting strengthens short-term memory.
The letters were lost because counting is too similar to remembering letters.
The letters were lost only because the participant was not paying attention to the screen.
college.why: Peterson and Peterson concluded that short-term memory fades quickly without rehearsal. Counting does not strengthen memory, and they judged it too dissimilar to the letters to cause interference.

simple.stem: What did Peterson and Peterson (1959) conclude from the Brown-Peterson task about short-term memory?
options: It fades quickly without rehearsal.
It lasts indefinitely without rehearsal.
It is lost only through interference.
It is unaffected by the length of a delay.
simple.why: The longer the distraction, the worse the recall, and they concluded that short-term memory fades without rehearsal. The other options deny that fading.

college.stem: A participant hears a list of words and a second participant looks at the same words silently. For which items would the modality effect predict an advantage for the first participant?
options: The last one or two items on the list.
The first one or two items on the list.
The items in the exact middle of the list.
Every item on the list to the same degree.
college.why: The effect is concentrated on the last one or two items. It is not an advantage for early, middle, or all items.

simple.stem: The modality effect is better memory for which part of a list?
options: The last one or two items of a heard list.
The first one or two items of a heard list.
The middle items of a seen list.
The whole list when it is seen.
simple.why: The effect is for the last items of a heard list compared with a silently viewed one.

college.stem: According to Neath and Surprenant (2003), why do people remember the final items of a heard list better than those of a list looked at silently?
options: Heard lists carry additional information about how the items sound, and that extra information aids recall of the end.
Heard lists are rehearsed less, and that reduced rehearsal protects the end of the list.
Heard lists activate a visual code, and that code strengthens the end of the list.
Heard lists are processed more slowly, and that slowness strengthens the beginning of the list.
college.why: The explanation is the extra sound information. Reduced rehearsal, a visual code, and slowed processing are not their account.

simple.stem: What did Neath and Surprenant (2003) propose to explain the modality effect?
options: Hearing gives extra sound information that helps the last items.
Hearing makes the first items easier to rehearse.
Seeing gives extra spatial information that helps the last items.
Seeing removes interference from the last items.
simple.why: They proposed that hearing provides additional information, how the list sounds. The other options are not their proposal.

college.stem: Which description best matches the idea of sensory memory?
options: A brief back-up store holding raw sensory input that has not been analyzed yet.
A lasting store holding meanings and facts that have been analyzed thoroughly.
A speech-based store that is refreshed by an articulatory control process.
A store that holds only words and never holds sounds or images.
college.why: Sensory memory is a back-up store of raw, unanalyzed input. The other options describe long-term knowledge, the phonological loop, or an invented restriction.

simple.stem: What does sensory memory hold?
options: Raw, unanalyzed sensory input.
Facts stored for a lifetime.
Only speech-based codes.
Only the meanings of words.
simple.why: Sensory memory holds raw, unanalyzed input as a back-up store.

college.stem: People looked at a brief display and could report only a small part of it. Sperling (1960) disagreed with the idea that people only saw that much. What was his position?
options: People saw most of the display, but the limit came from recalling it before it faded.
People saw only as much as they could report, because that is all perception can take in.
People saw nothing clearly, so what they reported were guesses.
People saw the display perfectly and stored it permanently, so the limit came from a later test.
college.why: Sperling (1960) argued that a sensory store held almost everything and the limit arose from recall. Perceiving only the reported amount, guessing, and permanent storage are not his position.

simple.stem: What did Sperling (1960) say caused the limit on how much people could report from a brief glance?
options: The limit of recalling what was seen.
The limit of perceiving what was shown.
The limit of the screen size.
The limit of listening to instructions.
simple.why: He argued the limit came from recall, not perception.

college.stem: Why did Sperling (1960) have participants report just one cued part of a display rather than everything they saw?
options: Because asking for only a cued part avoids the limit on how much can be recalled, revealing how much was seen.
Because asking for only a cued part makes the display easier to look at.
Because asking for only a cued part increases how long the display stays on screen.
Because asking for only a cued part removes the need for any memory.
college.why: A cued partial report sidesteps the recall bottleneck, exposing what the sensory store held. It does not change the display, its duration, or the need for memory.

simple.stem: Why did Sperling (1960) ask for a report of only a cued part of the display?
options: To test how much of the display was available without a recall limit.
To make the display last longer.
To help people rehearse the display.
To make the display easier to read.
simple.why: Reporting just the cued part let researchers sample the display without the recall limit.

college.stem: A viewer glances at a grid of letters. If the cue arrives right away, the viewer reports a cued row almost perfectly. If the cue arrives after a delay, the viewer reports only a small number of letters. What explains this?
options: The visual image of the grid faded during the delay, so less was left to report.
The viewer saw only a few letters, so the cue could not matter.
The grid was stored permanently, so the delay only affected the viewer's motivation.
The cue made the viewer forget letters that were not in the cued row.
college.why: The sensory (iconic) store holds nearly everything but fades quickly. Seeing only a few letters, permanent storage, and cue-caused forgetting do not explain the immediate-cue advantage.

simple.stem: What happens to partial report accuracy when the cue is delayed?
options: It falls back to the usual low level.
It rises above the usual level.
It stays nearly perfect.
It falls to zero.
simple.why: Delayed cues bring performance back to the usual level, showing the store lasts only briefly.

college.stem: Which finding is an example of the position error effect?
options: Items that are recalled in the wrong place tend to be placed near their correct position.
Items that are recalled in the wrong place tend to be placed at random across the list.
Items that are recalled in the wrong place tend to be moved to the very end of the list.
Items that are recalled in the wrong place tend to be replaced by new items.
college.why: Order errors are systematic, and the item is retained with approximate position information. Random placement, end-of-list placement, and replacement do not capture that.

simple.stem: What is true of the order errors in the position error effect?
options: They are systematic, not random.
They are random, not systematic.
They happen only for the first item.
They happen only for the last item.
simple.why: Errors in order are systematic.

college.stem: A person recalls a list of letters and gets two letters swapped with their immediate neighbors. What does this pattern suggest about what the person remembered?
options: The person still knew roughly where each item belonged, so some order information was retained.
The person had forgotten the items entirely, so the swap was a lucky accident.
The person had no order information, so the letters landed in random places.
The person had only the sound of the items, so order was never stored.
college.why: Neighbor swaps are systematic errors that reflect approximate position information. They do not reflect random guessing or lost information.

simple.stem: What does a recalled item in a nearby but wrong position suggest?
options: The person kept approximate position information.
The person forgot the item completely.
The person guessed the item at random.
The person never saw the item.
simple.why: Near-miss placement shows partial position information is retained.

college.stem: A researcher counts an item as remembered only if it is recalled in exactly the right position. What important finding about order memory could this scoring conceal?
options: That errors are systematic and the item's approximate position is still known.
That errors are random and the item's position is completely unknown.
That errors occur only for items heard rather than seen.
That errors disappear when people count backward between items.
college.why: Strict scoring hides the fact that misplaced items usually land near where they belong. Random errors and modality or distraction effects are not implied.

simple.stem: Why can percent correct hide what people know about order?
options: It counts near-miss errors as complete forgetting.
It counts correct answers twice.
It ignores the items completely.
It measures only speech, not memory.
simple.why: Percent correct treats near-miss errors as total loss even though approximate position is retained.

college.stem: Shepard and Metzler (1971) asked people to judge whether two block shapes were identical or mirror images when one was turned. What did participants report doing, and what did it show?
options: They mentally rotated one shape until it matched the other, showing that rotating a mental image takes time.
They compared the names of the shapes, showing that mental images are really verbal.
They remembered each shape as a list of features, showing that rotation is unnecessary.
They guessed at random, showing that mental images are unreliable.
college.why: Participants said they mentally rotated one shape to match the other, and rotation took time, as it does for real objects. Verbal naming, feature lists, and guessing are not the conclusion.

simple.stem: What did Shepard and Metzler (1971) suggest about mental images?
options: Mental images are much like real images.
Mental images are quite different from real images.
Mental images are only words.
Mental images cannot be used for tasks.
simple.why: They suggested mental images behave like real images.

college.stem: In the task of Shepard and Metzler (1971), people judged whether two shapes were identical or mirror images when one was turned. What did turning one shape require people to do?
options: Mentally rotate one shape to compare it with the other, which let researchers see how rotation behaves.
Describe their mental image in words, which let researchers compare the descriptions.
Memorize each shape as a list of features, which made rotation unnecessary.
Guess at random, which showed that mental images are unreliable.
college.why: Turning one shape forces a mental rotation to compare them, revealing how mental imagery works. It does not call for verbal descriptions, feature lists, or guessing.

simple.stem: Why did the task of Shepard and Metzler (1971) turn one of the two shapes?
options: To force people to mentally rotate an image.
To make the shapes easier to name.
To make people use words.
To make the shapes look identical.
simple.why: Turning a shape forces mental rotation.

college.stem: A person counts the windows in their home by picturing it. Which conclusion fits the finding that mental images behave like real images?
options: The person can inspect the mental image much as they would look at a real scene.
The person cannot be using imagery, because mental images behave nothing like real ones.
The person's description of the image must match it exactly, because images are fully reliable.
The person is counting only words, because mental images are just verbal lists.
college.why: If mental images behave like real images, a task such as counting windows can be done by inspecting the image. The other options deny imagery or claim it is purely verbal.

simple.stem: If mental images behave like real images, how can a person count the windows in their home?
options: By inspecting a mental image of the home.
Only by recalling a list of words.
Only by looking at the real home.
Only by guessing.
simple.why: Mental images behave like real images, so they can be inspected to do tasks like counting.

college.stem: Why do people rely on heuristics when estimating how likely things are?
options: Because they are fast and usually good enough in everyday life, even though they sometimes lead to wrong judgments.
Because they are always more accurate than calculation, even though they are slower.
Because they guarantee correct answers, even though they ignore evidence.
Because they are required by laws of probability, even though they are costly.
college.why: Heuristics give up some accuracy for speed. They do not guarantee accuracy or beat calculation.

simple.stem: What do heuristics trade away for speed?
options: Accuracy of the judgment.
Memory for the details.
Attention to the words.
The use of any information.
simple.why: Heuristics sacrifice accuracy to gain speed.

college.stem: Which judgment is an example of the conjunction fallacy?
options: Rating it more likely that a person is a nurse and an athlete than that the person is a nurse.
Rating it more likely that a person is a nurse than that the person is a nurse and an athlete.
Rating it equally likely that a person is a nurse and that the person is an athlete.
Rating it unlikely that a person is a nurse because the description is short.
college.why: Judging A and B together as more likely than A alone is the conjunction fallacy. The second option is the correct logic, and the others do not compare a combination to a part.

simple.stem: What is the conjunction fallacy?
options: Thinking that A and B together are more likely than A alone.
Thinking that A alone is more likely than A and B together.
Thinking that A and B can never happen together.
Thinking that A is certain if B is certain.
simple.why: The fallacy is judging the combination as more likely than one part.

college.stem: In a study by Shafir, Smith, and Osherson (1990), participants judged a profiled person's likelihood of professions and activities. Which result matches the study?
options: Participants sometimes judged that having both features was more probable than having just one of them.
Participants correctly judged that having both features was never more probable than having one.
Participants judged that having one feature was impossible if the other was present.
Participants judged all features as unrelated to the description.
college.why: The study showed the conjunction fallacy in some circumstances. Always correct logic, impossibility judgments, and unrelatedness are not what it found.

simple.stem: What did Shafir, Smith, and Osherson (1990) find in their ratings of likelihood?
options: People sometimes rated a combination as more likely than one part of it.
People always rated a combination as less likely than its parts.
People rated all options as equally likely.
People did not rate anything.
simple.why: They found the conjunction fallacy in some circumstances.

college.stem: Why do the cards D and 3 fall short when testing the rule 'If a card has a D on one side, it has a 3 on the other side'?
options: The 3 can only confirm the rule, while the 7 could falsify it.
The 3 could falsify the rule, but the D cannot.
The 3 is unrelated to the rule, so it never needs checking, and the 7 can only confirm it.
The D and the 3 together can show the rule is wrong, so nothing else is needed.
college.why: A 3 can only fit the rule, whereas the 7 could reveal a D behind it and break the rule. D and 7 is the correct pair.

simple.stem: In the Wason Selection Task, people typically choose cards that can do what?
options: Only confirm the rule.
Falsify the rule.
Show that the cards are unrelated.
Change the rule.
simple.why: People typically choose D and 3, and the 3 can only confirm the rule.

college.stem: Wason and Shapiro (1971) gave people a rule with the same logic in an abstract version and in a familiar version. Which result did they report?
options: The familiar thematic version was much easier than the abstract version.
The abstract version was much easier than the familiar thematic version.
The two versions were equally easy, because they share the same logic.
Neither version could be solved by anyone.
college.why: Same logic, different content: experience made the thematic version much easier. The other options contradict that.

simple.stem: What did Wason and Shapiro (1971) find about thematic rules?
options: They were easier to test than abstract rules.
They were harder to test than abstract rules.
They were exactly as hard as abstract rules.
They were impossible to test.
simple.why: Thematic rules were easier because of relevant experience.

college.stem: A person easily checks whether a friend who borrowed a car filled the gas tank, but struggles to test an abstract card rule of the same form. What explains the difference?
options: Experience with the familiar situation helps, while the abstract rule must be tested with logic alone.
Familiar rules are harder, because everyday knowledge interferes with logic.
Abstract rules are easier, because they contain no distracting content.
The two rules differ in logic, so they should not be compared.
college.why: Relevant experience supports thematic rule testing, whereas abstract rules require logic alone. Familiar content is not harder, and the logic is the same.

simple.stem: Why is the borrowed car rule easier to test than the card rule?
options: People have relevant experience with it.
It has different logic.
It is more abstract.
It has fewer cards.
simple.why: Experience with the familiar situation makes the thematic rule easier.

college.stem: Which finding is an example of a framing effect?
options: People choose differently when the same choice is shown in two different ways.
People choose the same option whenever the same choice is shown in two different ways.
People choose differently only when the options offer different outcomes.
People choose the same option because they cannot tell options apart.
college.why: A framing effect is a different choice for the same situation shown two ways. Choosing the same, or differing because the outcomes differ, is not framing.

simple.stem: What does a framing effect show about decisions?
options: How a choice is worded can change the decision.
Only the options themselves matter.
People never change their minds.
People always choose the safest option.
simple.why: Framing shows that wording and context shape decisions.

college.stem: What does the design of showing one choice in two ways let researchers separate?
options: The influence of wording from the influence of the actual options.
The influence of memory from the influence of attention.
The influence of speech codes from the influence of visual codes.
The influence of experience from the influence of logic.
college.why: Equivalent options with different wording isolate the effect of framing. The other contrasts belong to other studies.

simple.stem: Why show the same choice in two different ways?
options: To see whether wording alone changes the decision.
To make the choice harder to remember.
To make people choose the same option.
To hide the options.
simple.why: Different wording on equivalent options tests the effect of framing.

college.stem: A shopper prefers 'a 90 percent fat-free' product to one labeled '10 percent fat' even though they are identical. What does this show?
options: That how a choice is framed shapes the decision, not just the options themselves.
That people always choose the product with the larger number.
That people cannot detect the identical content of two products.
That people choose by sound similarity of the labels.
college.why: Identical products with different wording lead to different preferences, a framing effect. The other explanations do not account for the wording difference.

simple.stem: A choice is worded as a gain to one group and as a loss to another group, and choices differ. What is this called?
options: A framing effect.
A modality effect.
A position error effect.
A phonological similarity effect.
simple.why: Different choices from different wording of equivalent options is a framing effect.

college.stem: A contestant picks a door in a three-door game. The host, who always opens a non-prize door, reveals an empty door. The contestant says the remaining two doors are 50-50. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: The first pick still has only a 1 in 3 chance, so the other closed door has a 2 in 3 chance.
The first pick has a 2 in 3 chance, so the other closed door has a 1 in 3 chance.
The host opens doors at random, so the remaining doors are equal.
The first pick becomes certain once any door is opened.
college.why: Opening an empty door does not change the 1 in 3 chance of the first pick, so the other door holds 2 in 3. Treating the doors as equal is a probability intuition error.

simple.stem: In the Monty Hall 3 Door problem, what is the best choice after Monty opens an empty door?
options: Switch to the other closed door.
Stay with your first door.
Pick a door at random.
Switch only half the time.
simple.why: Switching wins about two-thirds of the time.

college.stem: A contestant in the Monty Hall 3 Door problem says switching and staying are equally good because two doors remain. What mistake is this?
options: Treating the two remaining doors as equally likely, ignoring that the first pick keeps its original chance.
Believing the host moves the prize after the contestant chooses.
Believing the first pick is certain once a door is opened.
Believing the host opens doors at random, including the prize door.
college.why: The first pick still has only a one in three chance, so the other closed door holds the remaining chance. The contestant wrongly treats the two doors as equal.

simple.stem: Why is it a mistake to say the two remaining doors in the Monty Hall problem are equally likely?
options: The first pick keeps its original chance, so the other closed door holds the rest.
Both doors hold the prize.
The opened door still holds the prize.
The host moves the prize.
simple.why: The first pick keeps a one in three chance, so the other closed door has the remaining chance.

college.stem: Which pattern do people typically show when choosing between a sure outcome and a gamble?
options: They take the sure thing when the outcomes are gains and the gamble when the outcomes are losses.
They take the gamble when the outcomes are gains and the sure thing when the outcomes are losses.
They take the sure thing whether the outcomes are gains or losses.
They take the gamble whether the outcomes are gains or losses.
college.why: People typically avoid risk with gains and seek risk with losses. The other patterns reverse or flatten it.

simple.stem: How do people typically choose between a sure outcome and a gamble for gains versus losses?
options: Sure thing for gains, gamble for losses.
Gamble for gains, sure thing for losses.
Sure thing for both.
Gamble for both.
simple.why: People avoid risk with gains and seek risk with losses.

college.stem: A shopper can take a guaranteed discount or a coupon that might give a bigger discount or nothing, with the same average value. Based on the typical pattern, which will most shoppers choose?
options: The guaranteed discount, because people usually avoid risk with gains.
The coupon, because people usually seek risk with gains.
The coupon, because people usually prefer the larger possible discount whatever the odds.
Either at random, because the pattern does not apply to discounts.
college.why: A discount is a gain, and people typically take the sure thing for gains. Seeking risk is the typical pattern for losses.

simple.stem: Offered a sure gain or a gamble with the same average value, what do people typically choose?
options: The sure gain.
The gamble.
Whichever is listed first.
Nothing.
simple.why: People avoid risk with gains, so they take the sure thing.

college.stem: In an experiment by German and Defeyter (2000), children had to turn a box over and use it as a support to help a toy bear reach a toy on a high shelf. Some children had first seen the box used as a container. How did the 5-year-olds perform in that condition?
options: They were not slowed by the earlier container use and were faster than the older children.
They were slowed more than the older children by the earlier container use.
They were slowed just as much as the older children by the earlier container use.
They failed to solve the task after seeing the container use, unlike older children.
college.why: German and Defeyter (2000) found 5-year-olds immune to the container demonstration; 6- and 7-year-olds were slower.

simple.stem: German and Defeyter (2000) showed some children a box being used as a container before asking them to use it as a support. Which children were NOT slowed by this?
options: Five-year-olds were not slowed by the container use.
Seven-year-olds were not slowed by the container use.
Six-year-olds were not slowed by the container use.
Every age group was slowed by the container use.
simple.why: The 5-year-olds were immune; 6- and 7-year-olds were slower after the container use.

college.stem: A person cannot see that a box could be used as a platform because they think of it only as a container. What is this called?
options: Functional fixedness, being stuck on an object's usual function and missing another possible use.
Perseveration, repeating an earlier response after the situation has changed.
Insight, suddenly seeing the whole solution after being stuck.
Attribute substitution, answering an easier question in place of a harder one.
college.why: This is functional fixedness. The other terms are different concepts.

simple.stem: What is functional fixedness?
options: Being stuck on an object's usual function and failing to see new uses.
Being unable to remember where an object was last placed.
Choosing the first option offered in a decision.
Solving a problem by suddenly seeing the answer.
simple.why: Functional fixedness means being stuck on an object's usual function.

college.stem: Why did German and Defeyter (2000) test some children after showing the box used as a container and others without that experience?
options: To see whether showing the usual container use slowed children from seeing the box as a support.
To see whether children liked the toy bear more after seeing the container use.
To see whether children could remember the box from one day to the next.
To see whether children preferred containers to supports when given a choice.
college.why: The container demonstration tests whether the usual function interferes; the no-demonstration condition shows baseline improvement with age.

simple.stem: What was the container demonstration in the box task meant to test?
options: Whether seeing the box's usual use makes it harder to use it as a support.
Whether children can lift heavy boxes without help.
Whether children remember a toy bear's name.
Whether children enjoy playing with boxes.
simple.why: It tests functional fixedness: whether the usual function interferes with a new use.

college.stem: Leist and colleagues (2022) played speech to be ignored while children and adults remembered either words in order or locations in order. Which result did they obtain?
options: Speech hurt memory for the verbal order task but spatial order memory was not disrupted.
Speech hurt memory for the verbal and spatial tasks about equally.
Speech hurt spatial order memory but left verbal order memory unaffected.
Speech hurt only the adults, in both the verbal and the spatial tasks.
college.why: The speech effect was specific to verbal material in Leist and colleagues (2022).

simple.stem: What did Leist and colleagues (2022) find when ignored speech was played during verbal and spatial memory tasks?
options: It hurt verbal memory but not spatial memory.
It hurt spatial memory but not verbal memory.
It hurt both kinds of memory equally.
It hurt neither kind of memory.
simple.why: Speech impaired verbal but not spatial recall.

college.stem: Which speech disrupts serial recall most in the irrelevant speech effect?
options: Changing-state speech, made of different syllables, disrupts recall more than repeated-syllable speech.
Steady-state speech, made of one repeated syllable, disrupts recall more than changing speech.
Speech played in a language the listener understands, but only if it is loud.
Speech that the listener attends to closely, regardless of its syllables.
college.why: Changing-state speech (different syllables) disrupts recall more than steady-state speech.

simple.stem: What is changing-state speech?
options: Speech made of different syllables that change from one to the next.
Speech made of one syllable repeated over and over.
Speech that gets louder over time.
Speech that the listener is asked to remember.
simple.why: Changing-state speech has different syllables; steady-state speech repeats one syllable.

college.stem: What did the spatial memory task let Leist and colleagues (2022) tell apart?
options: Whether speech disrupts memory for order of any kind or only for verbal material.
Whether children or adults have better hearing for ignored speech.
Whether steady-state speech is louder than changing-state speech.
Whether verbal memory is stored in a different country than spatial memory.
college.why: The spatial task separates accounts predicting disruption for any item from one limited to verbal material.

simple.stem: Why include a spatial memory task in a study of ignored speech?
options: To check whether speech disrupts only verbal memory or all kinds of memory.
To make the task easier for the children taking part.
To test whether the participants can hear the speech.
To keep the experiment shorter.
simple.why: Spatial items show whether the speech effect is specific to verbal material.

college.stem: What is cognitive offloading?
options: Using actions such as writing things down to reduce the mental demands of a task.
Repeating a list silently so that it stays active in the mind.
Forgetting information on purpose because it is no longer needed.
Grouping items into larger meaningful chunks to remember more.
college.why: Cognitive offloading means using external actions to reduce mental demands.

simple.stem: What is cognitive offloading?
options: Using actions like writing things down to reduce mental effort.
Repeating items silently to remember them.
Forgetting things on purpose.
Grouping items into chunks.
simple.why: Offloading uses external actions to reduce mental demands.

college.stem: In the work of Morrison and Richmond (2020), how did the length of a letter list relate to offloading?
options: Longer lists made people offload more, and offloading helped most for the longer lists.
Longer lists made people offload less, and offloading helped most for the shorter lists.
List length did not change how much people offloaded or how much it helped.
Longer lists made offloading harmful, so memory-only recall was better.
college.why: Offloading increased with load and benefited memory most at high loads.

simple.stem: What did Morrison and Richmond (2020) find about offloading when lists got longer?
options: People offloaded more and it helped more.
People offloaded less and it helped less.
People offloaded the same amount at every length.
People offloaded more but it made memory worse.
simple.why: Offloading and its benefit both grew with load.

college.stem: Which pattern did Morrison and Richmond (2020) report about memory ability and offloading?
options: Memory ability did not predict who offloaded.
Weaker memory ability strongly predicted who offloaded.
Stronger memory ability predicted who offloaded.
Memory ability predicted offloading only in the longest lists.
college.why: No link between memory ability and who offloaded was found.

simple.stem: Did memory ability predict who offloaded in the work of Morrison and Richmond (2020)?
options: No, memory ability did not predict who offloaded.
Yes, weaker memory predicted more offloading.
Yes, stronger memory predicted more offloading.
Yes, but only for the shortest lists.
simple.why: Memory ability did not predict offloading.

college.stem: What is one explanation for the intuitive error on the bat-and-ball problem?
options: Reasoners unconsciously swap in an easier problem and neglect the words 'more than'.
Reasoners deliberately choose the wrong answer to save time.
Reasoners cannot do the arithmetic needed to find the right answer.
Reasoners misremember the total cost of the bat and ball.
college.why: One account is unconscious attribute substitution.

simple.stem: What is attribute substitution?
options: Swapping in an easier question for the harder one that was asked.
Replacing a missing object with a similar one.
Choosing the option that was preselected.
Repeating a response that worked before.
simple.why: Attribute substitution means answering an easier problem without noticing.

college.stem: What did Hoover and Healy (2019) conclude about how people make the bat-and-ball error?
options: The error is conscious: people notice and remember the words 'more than' but do not use their meaning.
The error is unconscious: people never notice the words 'more than' at all.
The error is arithmetic: people cannot subtract and divide correctly.
The error is due to confidence: people simply guess without looking at the problem.
college.why: Incorrect reasoners recalled and recognized the phrase but did not integrate its meaning.

simple.stem: What did Hoover and Healy (2019) find about the wrong answer to the bat-and-ball problem?
options: People remembered the words 'more than' but did not use their meaning.
People never noticed the words 'more than'.
People could not do the arithmetic.
People guessed without looking at the problem.
simple.why: The phrase was recalled but its meaning was not integrated.

college.stem: Why use a control problem without the words 'more than'?
options: To check whether reasoners who answered wrongly were less confident when the phrase was present.
To check whether reasoners can do arithmetic when there are no words.
To check whether reasoners read faster when problems are shorter.
To check whether the cost of the bat and ball affects confidence.
college.why: The control lacks the phrase, so any confidence drop on the standard problem can be tied to it.

simple.stem: What did the control problem without 'more than' show about incorrect reasoners?
options: They were less confident on the standard problem than on the control.
They were more confident on the standard problem than on the control.
They were equally confident on both problems.
They solved the control problem correctly every time.
simple.why: Lower confidence on the standard problem showed they sensed something was wrong.

college.stem: In the work of Giuliani and colleagues (2023), which default changed choices?
options: Making the risky option the default increased risk taking.
Making the sure option the default increased risk aversion.
Making either option the default changed choices equally.
Neither default changed choices at all.
college.why: A risky default raised risk taking; a sure default did not raise risk aversion.

simple.stem: What did Giuliani and colleagues (2023) find when the risky option was the default?
options: People took more risks.
People took fewer risks.
People took the same risks as with no default.
People refused to choose anything.
simple.why: A risky default raised risk taking.

college.stem: Giuliani and colleagues (2023) asked people afterward where they thought a default came from. Which belief went with rejecting the default most often?
options: Seeing the default as what previous respondents chose or as the result of chance.
Seeing the default as the most rational choice.
Seeing the default as the safest and surest option.
Seeing the default as a mistake in the survey.
college.why: Those who thought the default came from previous respondents or chance tended to reject it most often.

simple.stem: Which belief about a default went with people rejecting it most often?
options: That it came from previous respondents or from chance.
That it was the most rational choice.
That it was the safest option.
That it was a mistake in the survey.
simple.why: Seeing the default as coming from previous respondents or chance went with rejecting it most often.

college.stem: What did Chein and colleagues (2011) conclude about how peers raise risk taking in adolescents?
options: The peer effect went with more activity in the brain's reward circuitry, while cognitive-control regions did not change.
The peer effect went with less activity in cognitive-control regions, while reward circuitry did not change.
Peers directly pressure adolescents, which shows up in motor regions of the brain.
Peers have no effect on the brain, so the extra risk comes from boredom.
college.why: Reward regions responded to peers; cognitive-control regions did not change with peer presence.

simple.stem: What did Chein and colleagues (2011) find happens in the adolescent brain when friends watch?
options: Reward-related brain regions become more active.
Cognitive-control brain regions become less active.
Visual brain regions become more active.
Nothing changes in the brain.
simple.why: Peers enhanced reward-circuit activity.

college.stem: What did the 'alone' condition give Chein and colleagues (2011) to compare with the 'friends watching' condition?
options: A baseline showing how much peer presence changes risk taking and brain activity.
A baseline showing how skilled each person is at real-world driving.
A baseline showing how much each person likes the friends who watch.
A baseline showing how fast the brain scanner collects data.
college.why: Alone versus watched shows the specific change caused by peers.

simple.stem: Why compare playing alone with playing while friends watched?
options: To see what changes in risk taking when peers are present.
To see which friends are better drivers.
To see how tired people get.
To see which game is harder.
simple.why: The comparison isolates the effect of peer presence.
